items_missed: Never qualified the destination type until minute 6 — spent the entire call building a profile, then discovered the drop-off was a U-Haul pod leaving the state and had to decline. 'Is this going into a pod or a storage unit that stays on site?' belonged in the first 60 seconds, right after 'is this a home, apartment or storage.'

Customer opened with 'I need moving service for this Monday, August 21st' — on a call dated Aug 28. Chris quoted a 12:30-2:30 Monday window without ever reconciling the date. He confirmed availability for a day he and the customer may not have agreed on.

No No Worries Damage Coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee. None of the three differentiators surfaced.
No clock explanation at all — no on-site start, no 2.5 hour minimum, no 15-minute proration.

top_strength: The access and logistics probing was genuinely strong and better than most calls at this branch. He got the 4th-floor unit, confirmed the elevator could be reserved, and then pushed one level deeper on how long it could be held — 'some apartments only give like two hour windows which is sometimes difficult to line up with' — which is exactly the kind of variable that blows up a move estimate. He also measured walk distance in real terms, translating 'a couple of feet' into '9 or 10 apartment doors' and 'within twenty feet, give or take like a two car length.' When the customer pushed back on the pod decline with 'Oh, why is that?', he gave a clear, calm, non-defensive liability explanation and she ended the call saying 'no worries, thank you so much.'
coaching_note: Chris, the single highest-leverage fix is qualifying order. You already ask 'is this a home, apartment or storage' about the pickup — ask the same thing about the drop-off in the same breath: 'And where's it going — a house, an apartment, or a storage unit? And if storage, is it a unit that stays on site, or a pod or container that gets hauled off later?' That one question, 30 seconds in, saves you the six minutes of profile-building you spent on a job we can't take, and it saves the customer her time too. Second priority: when we can't take a job, don't just end the call — convert it. She's still moving, she's still going to a U-Haul facility, and she was gracious about the decline. 'We can't load a pod that's leaving the state, but here's what we CAN do — if you rent an on-site unit at that facility instead, we'll move you right into it. Want me to price that out?' A decline is your warmest possible lead. Third, smaller but free: you had her spell her last name letter by letter and then never said it once. Use it three times before you hang up, and open with 'How are you today?' — right now the call reads as data entry, not a conversation. Methodology note for the record: this call was graded as a full_sales_call, and Pricing, Clock, Estimate, Save Your Ass and Booking were scored at low partial credit rather than granted as N/A. The job was legitimately declined, but the decline landed at minute 6 because of sequencing, not because the call type excluded those sections — so the transcript shows no evidence of those skills and the score reflects that.
phone_presence_notes: Almost entirely mechanical — 'Okay,' 'Okay, got it,' 'And then' carry the whole call, with zero name use, no 'how are you,' no affirmations, and no acknowledgment when the customer got confused about whether he wanted her legal name.
